claim: An estimated 312.9 million operations were performed worldwide in 2012, a 33.6% increase over eight years, with the largest proportional growth in the countries spending least per capita on health care [@weiser2015].
note: 312.9 million operations in 2012, 33.6% increase over 8 years, largest proportional increase in countries spending US$400 or less per capita.

claim: In a US national survey of adults who had undergone surgery, 86% reported postoperative pain, and three-quarters of those described it as moderate or extreme in the immediate postoperative period; 88% received analgesic medication, and 80% of those reported adverse effects from it [@gan2014].
note: ~86% had pain; 75% of these moderate/extreme immediately; 88% received analgesics, 80% of these had adverse effects.

claim: Contemporary registry data show the problem persists at scale and beyond that setting: among 26,193 adults in a Chinese national postoperative pain registry, 48.7% reported moderate-to-severe pain on the first postoperative day and 68% received systemic opioids [@liu2023china].
note: 26,193 adults; 48.7% moderate-to-severe pain on POD1; systemic opioid use 68%.

claim: Poorly controlled postoperative pain and the drugs used to treat it both contribute to delayed recovery, prolonged hospitalisation and avoidable morbidity [@kehlet2003].
note: The review links pain, nausea, ileus and other surgical sequelae to complications, hospital treatment and delayed convalescence; the attribution to the analgesic drugs themselves is the authors' synthesis rather than a stated finding.

claim: In a US cohort of previously opioid-naive adults, new persistent opioid use occurred in 5.9% after minor and 6.5% after major surgery, against 0.4% in a non-operative comparison cohort [@brummett2017].
note: Minor 5.9% vs major 6.5%; non-operative cohort 0.4% (Results).

claim: A subsequent meta-analysis of 43 observational studies (6,507,173 participants) reached a comparable pooled estimate of 7.15% (95% CI 6.02–8.38) but with a 95% prediction interval of 1.34–17.02%, again found no significant variation by surgery type, and showed the figure to be strongly definition-dependent: 8.29% under a 90–180-day definition against 2.89% where opioid use across a full 180-day period was required [@frangakis2026].
note: 43 studies, 6,507,173 participants; 7.15% (6.02–8.38); PI 1.34–17.02%; no difference by surgery type; 8.29% vs 2.89% by definition.

claim: Estimates are also markedly lower outside the United States — 1.7% of 642,857 procedures in a national Austrian cohort of 559,096 patients [@bologheanu2025] — and a pooled analysis restricted to opioid-naive participants at baseline gave 1.2% (95% CI 0.4–3.9) [@lawal2020].
note: Bologheanu: 10,810 cases (1.7%) among 642,857 procedures in 559,096 patients; the sentence was corrected on 2026-09-28 to name procedures as the denominator. Lawal: 1.2% (0.4–3.9) in opioid-naive restricted analyses.

claim: The firmer case for opioid sparing is the immediate one: opioid side-effects, tolerance and opioid-induced hyperalgesia are dose-related, and multiple clinical guidelines now endorse multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia on that basis [@adams2023].
note: Side-effects, tolerance and opioid-induced hyperalgesia, and guideline endorsement of multimodal analgesia, are in the abstract; "dose-related" is not stated in the abstract.

claim: Electrical stimulation at acupuncture points releases endogenous opioid peptides in a frequency-dependent pattern, with low-frequency stimulation favouring enkephalin and β-endorphin and high-frequency stimulation favouring dynorphin [@han2003; @han2004], and is also associated with anti-inflammatory and autonomic effects [@lin2022; @wang2021].
note: Han 2004: 2 Hz releases enkephalin, beta-endorphin and endomorphin; 100 Hz dynorphin (Han 2003 has no abstract; title states frequency-dependent neuropeptide release). Lin 2022 and Wang 2021 describe anti-inflammatory and autonomic/HPA mechanisms.

claim: Reviews to date have generally pooled heterogeneous modalities into a single estimate [@wu2016review; @liu2025review]; one recent meta-analysis of electrical acupoint stimulation for postoperative nausea and vomiting pooled electroacupuncture and transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation into a combined effect and reported the two only as subgroups of it [@lu2023review], although their sham comparators are not interchangeable and their mechanisms of delivery differ.
note: Wu 2016 pooled acupuncture, EA and TEAS with subgroups; Lu 2023 pooled EA and TEAS for PONV with modality subgroups (confirmed). Liu 2025 pooled 25 "acupuncture" trials; the abstract does not list the modalities, so "heterogeneous modalities" for Liu 2025 rests on the full text, not re-checked here.

claim: Syntheses restricted to TEAS exist but are confined to single surgical populations and do not isolate absolute opioid consumption: one in gynaecological surgery pooled sham-controlled and conventional-analgesia comparisons and found no significant reduction in pain intensity at low-to-moderate certainty [@tahmasbi2025], and the most recent, in cancer surgery, reported pain as a standardised mean difference across mixed comparators rather than in absolute units [@chu2026].
note: Tahmasbi: 10 RCTs in gynaecological surgery; sham or conventional-analgesic comparators; pain reduction not significant; low-to-moderate certainty. Chu 2026: cancer surgery; pain as SMD; the abstract says "control group" without detailing comparator types.

claim: A systematic review of 570 analgesic trials after hip and knee arthroplasty found a median clinician-perceived threshold of 10 mg intravenous morphine equivalents over 0–24 hours (interquartile range 6.8–14.5), and 40% for relative reductions (interquartile range 30–50%), while noting that 46% of trials with statistically significant primary outcomes did not reach their own predetermined threshold [@laigaard2021].
note: 570 trials; median 10 mg IV morphine equivalents 0–24 h (IQR 6.8–14.5); relative 40% (IQR 30–50%); 46% of significant trials below their own MCID.

claim: Thresholds for opioid consumption are not interchangeable with those for pain intensity [@myles2017], and an apparent opioid reduction accompanied by worse pain is not opioid sparing.
note: Myles gives the pain-VAS MCID (about 10 on 100 mm); the statement that opioid and pain thresholds are not interchangeable is the authors' inference from the separate thresholds.
